paragraphs.text: An [oolong](oolong:definition) from Beipu, in Hsinchu County, made in 1977. Hsinchu shares [Oriental Beauty](taiwan-oolong:definition) with Miaoli, and like all of [Taiwan's oolong](taiwan-oolong:history) this tea traces back to the plants and craft that settlers brought over from Fujian.

Taiwan keeps oolong for years and calls it [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Tea chosen for keeping starts well roasted and dry. The keeper roasts it again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says when an oolong becomes old, and those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years. At forty-nine years, this one is well past that.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
